assessment.nobel_worthiness: Optical lattice clocks, trapping neutral atoms at the magic wavelength so that Doppler and recoil shifts vanish, opened fractional frequency uncertainties near 1e-18. This is precision atomic physics at its best: a new way of controlling atoms that reveals physics (gravitational redshift over millimetres, tests of constancy of constants, a path to redefining the second). Clear, original and lasting.
assessment.attribution: Katori made the 2001-2003 magic-wavelength proposal and the first Sr lattice clock; Jun Ye drove the systematic accuracy and many-body/clock-comparison advances. The two-name credit is clean and fair; Hall and Hansch were already honoured for the comb that underpins it, and I am not aware of a comparable disputed third contributor, though others (e.g. Lemonde, Gill) contributed in parallel.
assessment.maturity: Strongly confirmed by many independent laboratories worldwide (Sr, Yb, Hg), with agreement across continents and fibre-link comparisons. The interpretation is stable and recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Whether the committee would view this as sufficiently distinct from earlier clock and comb recognition (2005, 2012).
Priority issues among Sr/Yb groups and the optical-clock community beyond the two named people are only partly known to me.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Ultracold atoms in optical lattices realised the Hubbard model with tunable parameters, including the superfluid-to-Mott-insulator transition, and made quantum many-body systems directly observable, with single-site imaging. It answers fundamental questions about correlated quantum matter using the atomic physics toolbox I know well; a genuine new capability with broad impact.
assessment.attribution: The Jaksch-Zoller proposal (1998) and the Greiner-Bloch Mott-insulator experiment (2002) are the decisive pair; Cirac and Dalibard also made important contributions, so the five-name credit forces a hard choice. Selecting Bloch, Greiner and Zoller is defensible but leaves out Jaksch (not on the list), Cirac and Dalibard, and the Hansch/Esslinger/Bloch lineage.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many independent groups with consistent results, and the quantum simulation programme has matured for two decades. Timing is good, though the claim of useful simulation beyond classical reach is still developing.
uncertainties: Overlap with BEC (2001) and optical-lattice Nobel contexts could make the committee view this as extension rather than a new discovery.
Division of credit among theory and experiment among five credited names is unresolved.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Atom interferometry makes matter waves into precision instruments, measuring gravity, rotation and fundamental constants (fine-structure constant, G) with extraordinary sensitivity. It sits at the intersection of quantum mechanics and metrology and illustrates the wave nature of massive objects. Deep, original and with clear impact on precision measurement.
assessment.attribution: Bordé (Ramsey-Bordé interferometer, theory of atom interferometry), Pritchard (first atom interferometers with nanostructure gratings, atomic beams) and Kasevich/Chu (laser-pulse interferometers; Chu already a laureate) are the decisive figures. The three-name credit looks workable, but Chu's Nobel overlap and contributions from Mlynek and Keith complicate it.
assessment.maturity: Well confirmed across many laboratories, including inertial sensors, gravity gradiometry and constant measurements; applications are emerging and agreement with theory is excellent. Mature and timely.
uncertainties: Overlap with the 1997 laser cooling Nobel and Chu's role may reduce perceived novelty.
Priority and credit among Bordé, Pritchard, Mlynek, Chu and Kasevich is not fully resolved in my memory.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The quantum spin Hall effect and Z2 topological insulators represent a new phase of matter distinguished by topology rather than symmetry breaking, with protected edge states. The idea is original, clear and has reshaped condensed matter physics. Fundamental understanding of a new state of matter, not technology-driven.
assessment.attribution: Kane and Mele predicted the Z2 phase (2005) and the quantum spin Hall effect in graphene; Molenkamp's group observed the effect in HgTe wells (2007) following the Bernevig-Hughes-Zhang proposal. Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang, Fu, Moore, Balents and Hasan (ARPES) are not in the credited names, so the credit is incomplete, though the trio is a plausible configuration.
assessment.maturity: Extensively confirmed by independent transport and ARPES experiments over almost two decades, with stable interpretation. Recognition is timely.
uncertainties: Several key contributors (Zhang, Bernevig, Fu, Hasan) fall outside the credited names, so fairness of the three-name configuration is uncertain.
I defer to condensed matter colleagues on how central the quantum spin Hall effect is relative to the 3D materials.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Aharonov-Bohm effect and Berry phase show that phases of wave functions carry physical, gauge-invariant information, a deeply fundamental concept that underlies molecular physics, atoms in fields, topological matter and quantum computing. It speaks to what quantum mechanics really says about the physical world.
assessment.attribution: Aharonov and Bohm (1959; Bohm is deceased and cannot be honoured) and Berry (1984), with Pancharatnam, Longuet-Higgins and Simon earlier or adjacent contributions. A two-person prize of Aharonov and Berry is workable but the Aharonov-Bohm effect is inseparable from Bohm, which makes the pairing awkward.
assessment.maturity: Both effects are verified in many experiments (Tonomura electron holography, molecular and optical Berry phases) and are textbook physics. The recognition is arguably late rather than premature.
uncertainties: The omission of Bohm and the independent prior work of Ehrenberg-Siday and Pancharatnam raise attribution questions.
Whether the committee finds the work sufficiently a discovery of nature rather than a theoretical concept.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The Cirac-Zoller proposal for quantum gates with trapped ions and its experimental realisation provide the first fully controllable quantum-computing architecture, with high-fidelity entangling gates and error correction demonstrations. It is a clear, original, technologically relevant link between atomic physics and quantum information.
assessment.attribution: Cirac and Zoller proposed the scheme (1995); Blatt, Wineland and Monroe made the decisive experimental demonstrations. Wineland already shared the 2012 prize, and Monroe is not in the credited names, so the experimental credit is partial. The trio is plausible but incomplete.
assessment.maturity: Many groups confirmed the gates and scaled up the platforms. The path to large-scale quantum computing remains open, which makes the claim of a computing breakthrough premature, though the physics is mature.
uncertainties: The recognition could be premature as long as scalable quantum computation has not been demonstrated.
Overlap with 2012 prize and with Cirac and Zoller in other candidates; Monroe and Wineland excluded from the credited names.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: Cavity optomechanics brought macroscopic mechanical oscillators into the quantum regime through ground-state cooling, squeezing and entanglement, addressing directly where the boundary between quantum and classical lies. This is close to what I find most interesting in the 2025 prize logic, yet the discovery is a body of work rather than one result.
assessment.attribution: Cleland and Martinis demonstrated a mechanical resonator in the quantum ground state (2010); Aspelmeyer and Kippenberg developed optomechanical cooling and the radiation-pressure theory and experiments. Teufel, Painter, Harris and Lehnert also made decisive contributions, so a three-person credit leaves out several people.
assessment.maturity: Confirmed by many groups using different platforms. However, the 2025 prize on macroscopic quantum effects in circuits has just recognised a neighbouring theme, so timing relative to that prize is delicate.
uncertainties: Contributions by Teufel, Painter, Harris and Lehnert are outside the credited names, so a fair three-person split is uncertain.
Possible redundancy with the 2025 award on macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits.

assessment.nobel_worthiness: The theoretical discovery that, in two dimensions, particles can have fractional exchange statistics between bosons and fermions is conceptually deep and original; it sets what particle identity means in quantum mechanics and underlies topological quantum computing ideas. It is a beautiful fundamental result.
assessment.attribution: Leinaas and Myrheim (1977) and Wilczek (1982) are the decisive theoretical papers, and the three-name credit looks complete for the theory; Wilczek is already a laureate (2004), which could complicate it. Halperin and Arovas-Schrieffer-Wilczek tied it to the quantum Hall effect.
assessment.maturity: Direct experimental confirmation of anyonic braiding statistics came only around 2020 (Fève, Manfra and others), which is recent, so the experimental evidence is real but not yet thoroughly replicated across independent laboratories. This makes the recognition somewhat early.
uncertainties: Experimental evidence is recent and from few groups, so independence of confirmation is limited.
Wilczek already holds a Nobel Prize; a separate prize on the experiments (B012) could be a cleaner configuration.
